ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows an isosceles triangle with apex A at the top and base BC at the bottom. Points M and N lie on the two equal slanted sides and are stated to be midpoints. The segment from M goes to the right base vertex C, and the segment from N goes to the left base vertex B; these two segments intersect at P. The left small triangle BMP is labeled area 3, the right small triangle CNP is labeled area 3, the lower triangle BCP is labeled area 6, and the top quadrilateral AMPN is marked with a question mark. Reasoning: Since M and N are midpoints, BN and CM are medians, so their intersection P is the centroid. Thus P lies one third of the altitude above the base BC, making area triangle BCP equal to one third of the whole triangle ABC. Since [BCP] = 6, the whole triangle has area [ABC] = 18. The unknown quadrilateral AMPN is the remaining area after subtracting the three labeled regions: 18 - 6 - 3 - 3 = 6.

method.method_draft: Let the isosceles triangle be ABC with apex A, base BC, M on AB and N on AC. From the image, read that M is joined to C and N is joined to B, intersecting at P; the three shown regions have areas [BMP]=3, [CNP]=3, and [BCP]=6, and the unknown marked quadrilateral is AMPN. From the text, use that M and N are midpoints of the equal sides, so by symmetry P lies on the altitude/median from A to BC. Since M and N are midpoints, the two cevians BM? Actually NB and MC meet at P at one third of the altitude above the base: in coordinates B=(-1,0), C=(1,0), A=(0,h), M=(-1/2,h/2), N=(1/2,h/2), the intersection of MC and NB is P=(0,h/3). Thus area triangle BCP is one third of the whole triangle ABC. The image gives [BCP]=6, so [ABC]=18. The unknown quadrilateral AMPN is the total area minus the three lower/side regions: 18 - 6 - 3 - 3 = 6.
